The Five Civilized Tribes. The Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole were five major Native American nations who lived in the southeastern United States and adopted elements of European American governmental, economic, and cultural practices during the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Named by American settlers who regarded their political structures, literacy, and agricultural systems as civilized by European standards, these tribes maintained internal sovereignty despite increasing pressure from United States expansion. However, they were forcibly removed from their homelands to Oklahoma during the eighteen thirties, an event memorialized as the Trail of Tears.

The Cherokee nation was the largest of the five, occupying the Appalachian region in present-day Carolinas and Tennessee, and developed a syllabary script created by Sequoyah. The Choctaw nation occupied present-day Mississippi and Louisiana and was one of the first to be forcibly relocated westward in eighteen thirty-one. The Creek nation occupied the southeastern coastal plain and signed treaties with the United States but were eventually displaced. The Chickasaw nation occupied present-day Tennessee, Kentucky, and Mississippi, fiercely resisting removal but displaced by the eighteen thirties. The Seminole nation occupied Florida and resisted removal longest, leading to the prolonged Seminole Wars from eighteen seventeen to eighteen fifty-eight before final displacement.

The term civilized reflected only American prejudices. These were complex, sovereign nations with sophisticated legal systems, written laws, and trade networks.
